solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Harsh Dickensian Dr — niggard, sadly

indicators.note: sadly suggests the letters have come to a sorry, disordered state, so they are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, the abbreviation for doctor

explanation.surface: A grim Dickens doctor is described as a miser, which is a shame.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sadly' shuffles DR plus NIGGARD into the name.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Gradgrind is the fact-obsessed, severe schoolmaster in Dickens's novel Hard Times.

clue.text: Endlessly pant for air

indicators.note: without its end, so the final letter of the synonym is dropped

parts.note: to pant is to gasp for breath

explanation.surface: Someone out of breath is gasping for oxygen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endlessly' cuts the P off GASP.
explanation.definitionFit: Air is a mixture of gases, and in everyday speech a gas is any airlike substance.

clue.text: Nearly all with a second mission

indicators.note: nearly the whole word, so its last letter is lost

parts.note: taken as the word ALL
MO is short for moment, a second

explanation.surface: Almost everyone joining a second missionary outpost.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nearly' trims ALL to AL.
explanation.definitionFit: The Alamo in San Antonio, Texas, was originally a Spanish Catholic mission before its famous siege.

clue.text: Windiest in August, I established

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: Someone claims to have found that August is the breeziest month.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' points to the answer concealed in auGUST I ESTablished.
explanation.definitionFit: Gusty describes weather with strong blasts of breeze, so the superlative means most blustery.

clue.text: Stupidity of ten caught in awful DIY

indicators.note: the ten and the caught are placed inside the jumbled letters
awful suggests a botched job, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: IO looks like the figures 10
C is the cricket abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: Ten people caught out by dreadful home-improvement work, a foolish business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'awful' jumbles the home-improvement letters and 'in' sets the other pieces inside them; ten is drawn as the figures 1 and 0.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiocy is utter foolishness, a straightforward synonym for stupidity.

clue.text: Pass on first of tips in attempt to lose weight

parts.note: to pass on is a euphemism for to die

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the following word is used

explanation.surface: Advice to skip the leading tip when trying to slim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first of' takes T from tips.
explanation.definitionFit: A diet is a regime of restricted eating undertaken to slim down.

clue.text: Tom, perhaps, starts off cold, afterwards tender

indicators.note: the beginnings of the next three words are taken

explanation.surface: Tom, maybe, begins cold then becomes gentle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'starts off' picks C, A and T.
explanation.definitionFit: A tom is a male feline, so tom is an example of the animal.

clue.text: Wind round and round, in crack

indicators.note: the two rounds are placed inside the gap

parts.note: a chink is a narrow crack or opening
O is round in shape
a second O, also round in shape

explanation.surface: A breeze swirling round and round through a gap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts OO inside CHINK.
explanation.definitionFit: The chinook is a warm, dry westerly that blows down the eastern Rockies.

clue.text: Article, black, prepared for wealthy people

parts.note: THE is the definite article
jet means deep glossy black
set means ready or prepared

explanation.surface: A newspaper item about something dark made ready for the rich.
explanation.definitionFit: The jet set are fashionable rich travellers who fly between glamorous resorts.

clue.text: Boxes, mostly thin on the ground

indicators.note: most of the word is kept, its final letter dropped

parts.note: sparse means scarce or thin on the ground

explanation.surface: Cardboard cartons are in short supply.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' cuts the last E off SPARSE.
explanation.definitionFit: To spar is to box in practice, trading light punches, so spars means fights with fists.

clue.text: Catalogue is quite miserable, being somewhat reduced

indicators.note: only a stretch from inside these words survives, the ends trimmed away

explanation.surface: A catalogue looks rather glum after being cut down in size.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being somewhat reduced' leaves ITEMISE from quITE MISErable.
explanation.definitionFit: To itemise is to list things one by one, as a catalogue does.

clue.text: Region for French wine: borders of Champagne

parts.note: pro means in favour of, for
vin is French for wine

indicators.note: only the outer letters of the next word are used

explanation.surface: An area known for its French wines, on the edge of Champagne.
explanation.walkthrough: 'borders of' gives CE from Champagne.
explanation.definitionFit: A province is an administrative territory or area within a country.

clue.text: Pleasant friend getting a place in restaurant

parts.note: pal is informal for a friend
a table is where a diner is seated

explanation.surface: A nice mate manages to book somewhere to eat.
explanation.definitionFit: Palatable means agreeable to taste or acceptable, so broadly agreeable.

clue.text: Solid fuel, fine stored in church

indicators.note: one piece is kept inside the other

parts.note: CE is Church of England
OK means fine, all right

explanation.surface: Coal-type fuel is kept in the church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stored in' signals one piece inside the other; fine is not a penalty here but means all right.
explanation.definitionFit: Coke is the carbon residue left when coal is heated, burnt as smokeless fuel.

clue.text: Young creature: I'm holding her little angels!

indicators.note: the young animal grips the pronoun inside it

parts.note: a cub is a young animal such as a fox or bear
taken as written without the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A parent clutching a child and calling the kids little angels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'holding' makes the young animal wrap round the pronoun; the exclamation is a fond parent's sigh, while the definition is literal.
explanation.definitionFit: Cherubim are the order of angels, pictured in art as chubby winged children.

clue.text: Girl, behold, one in America

parts.note: lo is an old word meaning look or behold

indicators.note: the numeral is placed inside the country

parts.note: USA is the United States of America
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Look, a young woman, one of a kind, over in the States.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts I inside USA.
explanation.definitionFit: Louisa is a female given name, so an example of a girl's name.

clue.text: Relaxed after countries coming together are insulting

parts.note: the UN, United Nations, is countries joined in one body
to wound is to hurt someone's feelings, as an insult does; here it stands as the past form, hurt

explanation.surface: People calm down once nations unite, though they are rude.
explanation.walkthrough: UN comes first; 'after' just sets the order of the surface phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Unwound means calmed down, eased of tension, like a slackened spring.

clue.text: Rocks passed in the middle, concealing fish

indicators.note: the middle pair hides the fish between them
only the central letters of the word are taken

parts.note: hake is a sea fish of the cod family

explanation.surface: Stones went past in the middle, hiding a fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in the middle' takes the central pair of passed, and 'concealing' wraps them round the fish; Rocks is a verb, not stones.
explanation.definitionFit: To rock is to sway or jolt, the same as to shake.

clue.text: Her SAE transported in black car?

indicators.note: moved about, so the letters are carried into a new order

explanation.surface: Her stamped addressed envelope is carried in a dark vehicle.
explanation.walkthrough: SAE is a British stamped addressed envelope; 'transported' rearranges HER SAE. The question mark flags a definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: A hearse is the long vehicle, traditionally dark, that carries a coffin to a funeral.

clue.text: Urban area to west — and London's east end

indicators.note: the right-hand end of a word read on a map is the east, so its final letter is used

explanation.surface: A city district lies westward, and also in London's East End.
explanation.walkthrough: 'east end' is not the London district: it means the last letter of London, N.
explanation.definitionFit: A town is a built-up settlement, a populated urban place.

clue.text: Worn out, as mostly predicted, strangely

indicators.note: strangely means the letters come out oddly ordered
most of the word is used, its last letter dropped

explanation.surface: Exhausted, just about as forecast, oddly enough.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' gives PREDICTE; 'strangely' rearranges it.
explanation.definitionFit: Decrepit describes something old, feeble and dilapidated.

clue.text: Forward Hearts found in Scottish city

parts.note: pert means cheeky, forward
H is the card-game abbreviation for hearts

explanation.surface: A Hearts striker turns up in a Scottish city; Hearts is an Edinburgh football club.
explanation.definitionFit: Perth is a city on the River Tay in central Scotland.

clue.text: Publicity notice detective sergeant puts on

parts.note: an ad is an advertisement
DS is the police abbreviation for detective sergeant

explanation.surface: A police officer places an advert.
explanation.definitionFit: To add is to include or attach more, so adds means places on.

clue.text: Blackguard's jumper

definitions.meaning: a dishonourable cad; read as blackguard is

explanation.surface: A villain's sweater.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jumper' suggests a British sweater; it is something that leaps.
explanation.definitionFit: A bounder is an old-fashioned word for a rogue, while one who bounds is a leaper.

clue.text: Poet's line recalled in good French

definitions.note: the possessive reads as 'Poet is', a contraction, so the noun answer still fits the whole clue as a statement

indicators.note: the turned line goes inside the French word

parts.note: bon is French for good

indicators.note: called back, so the line is turned round

parts.note: RY, railway, is a line

explanation.surface: A poet's verse remembered in fine French.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recalled' turns the railway line round and 'in' puts it inside the French word; line as railway is a stock crossword abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord Byron was the English Romantic poet who wrote Don Juan.

clue.text: Pinch secret code after turning up

indicators.note: in a down clue turning up reads the word from the bottom

parts.note: PIN is a personal identification number

explanation.surface: Steal a password after it surfaces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after turning up' reads PIN upward.
explanation.definitionFit: To nip is to squeeze sharply between fingers, the same action as a pinch.

clue.text: Stop a goal

explanation.surface: Halting a score.
explanation.definitionFit: To end is to cease, and an end is something one aims at.

clue.text: Titanic, possibly, the start of Hard Times: pa's awful!

indicators.note: awful signals a dreadful mess, so the letters are reordered
only the first letter of the next word

explanation.surface: A disaster begins in the Dickens novel Hard Times: father is dreadful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the start of' gives H; 'awful' rearranges H, TIMES and PAS.
explanation.definitionFit: The Titanic was a steam-driven ocean liner, so it is an example of the vessel.
